taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes the species appears to constitute a superspecies with Mallard and American Black Duck and is sometimes included in Mallard (AOU 1983).
fieldMarks: Both sexes look like a darker version of a female Mallard
Bill bright yellow (male) or dull yellow (female)
Blue wing patch (speculum) lacks the broad white borders of a Mallard
Body paler and head more buff than American Black Duck
behavior: Mostly non-migratory; makes local movements as habitat conditions change
Forages in shallow water, mostly dabbling at mud just below the surface, occasionally up-ending
Eats seeds of aquatic plants and grasses, insects, snails and occasionally small fish
Call is a loud quack like a Mallard's
habitat: Marshes and open marshy country, wet prairies and rice fields; favors treeless country. In coastal areas usually fresh or brackish ponds adjacent to the coast rather than salt marsh.
range: Two natural resident ranges: the western Gulf Coast from Alabama west to Texas and south to Tamaulipas, and the Florida peninsula. Populations introduced from the 1970s exist in eastern Georgia and eastern South Carolina.

lookalikes.name: Mallard (female)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mottled Duck is darker and its wing patch lacks Mallard's broad white borders.

lookalikes.name: American black duck
lookalikes.howToTell: Mottled Duck's body is paler and head more buff; Black Duck is rare in the deep south.

lookalikes.name: Mexican duck
lookalikes.howToTell: Compare in the Southwest, from southern and western Texas to Arizona.
